# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Trying a pair first (my matinee, Eleanor's noisy walk) and keeping up with many voices (Walter's family lunch, Ruth's audience questions) are two different things I'd recognise. Both names are plain, and Diego's cost complaint and Tomás's end-seat habit fit neither group, so leaving them alone is right.
whys.g2: There is no junk or explicit answer here, and Tomás's answer, which is off the question since it describes his seating workaround rather than what would make it worth more, is rightly kept out of the groups.

founder.order_why: Screen 14 (who else has to agree) comes after cost and price (12-13), splitting it from screen 10 (does the wearer decide or someone else), which asks nearly the same thing and should sit right beside it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 (who decides vs. who else has to agree) overlap, and 15-16 then re-check that same buyer/payer point; screens 3 and 4 carry the identical kicker and question, so they read as the same screen twice.
founder.missing: Price was asked as one figure, with no way to say what I actually sell: a one-off $599 pair of glasses plus an optional $20/month Pro plan. I had to fold it into a yearly range. It also never asked whether HSA/FSA money can pay for it, which for my buyers is a real part of who pays.

PRIMARY.missing: What I use today to keep up, like a captioning app on my phone, lipreading, hearing aids, or asking people to repeat, and what that costs me. Also where conversations break down most (restaurants, group talk, work meetings, the theatre) and whether glasses would work with my hearing aids or my own glasses.

screens.why4: The same deaf or hard-of-hearing adult appears twice, once as has the problem and once as decides to buy, which overlaps, and the Nobody else row carries no tag while the others do.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree, with no added roles like an audiologist or family member.
screens.why7: The card says the person with the problem and the decider are one row when they are the same person, but here they are split into two rows; otherwise Nobody else comes first, no roles are added, and the belief that nobody else has to agree can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: The people involved: Nobody else (no one has to agree) · Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult (has the problem, decides to buy)

screens.why1: Right after I named nobody else on the previous screens, it is natural to see the statement I will test and confirm it before moving on.
screens.why2: The title and belief are plain, but the bar's 'the last time they paid for something for this' needs a second read, because 'for this' never says for what, such as captions or hearing help.
screens.why3: Whether my wearers decide and pay on their own, with HSA/FSA, is something I know from my own customers.
screens.why4: The list holds only Nobody else, shown as a statement to confirm with a clear way back to name a role, which is the right shape for what I typed.
screens.why5: I picked Nobody else, and the belief says the wearer decides and nobody else must agree first, which is exactly what I meant.
screens.why7: With Nobody else tested, the belief matches my list, the bar counts only decided alone as support, and the four fixed answers can both support it and refute it, as the card requires.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but word the bar as: Holds if at least 2 in 3 deaf or hard-of-hearing adults say they decided on their own the last time they paid for something to help them follow conversations.

screens.why1: After who pays and the price, asking what first step I'd want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take before paying is the obvious next question for a $599 pair of glasses.
screens.why2: The question is clear, but the hint's examples, "pay for a pilot" and "let us run a trial", are business-sale words I'd never use for a person buying glasses for themselves, so I read it twice to see they didn't fit me.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I ask people to do first, which is order a pair on the 15-day risk-free return, so I can answer from my own funnel.
screens.why4: The one chip, I'm not sure, is the escape the card allows on the founder's side and it fits a box I type into.
screens.why5: My typed step, "order the caption glasses with free returns", sits in the box word for word, keeping free returns and the glasses.
screens.why7: The box asks for one step in base form within 9 words, says where the money goes, and promises a smaller free step on the next screen when the step costs money, which is what the card's step and smaller_step shape require; my answer meets it.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take, and what would it cost them? e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "try a pair at a clinic"

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, it's obvious I'd check how strangers will hear it and what smaller step Keel paired with it.
screens.why2: The served list reads cleanly, but the smaller-step line is garbled ('Yes, after Try the caption glasses in person first'), so I had to read it twice to see what Keel drafted.
screens.why3: Whether a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult would order glasses they can send back is exactly what my wearers decide for themselves; I pay attention to it every day.
screens.why4: There are two firm answers and two soft ones, all distinct and in plain words: order them, try them first, probably not, no.
screens.why5: My step is kept whole, including 'free returns' and 'caption glasses', but 'in person' is Keel's addition: I sell online with 15-day returns, so this promises a hands-on trial I never said we offer.
screens.why7: The first option is my own step in full, and the soft yes is a free step taken before it, different from ordering with returns; with nothing above the 1-in-3 bar and No as the floor, the belief can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Smaller step: 'Seeing the captions on a demo video first' -> 'Probably, after seeing the captions on a demo video first'; and fix the line to read 'Or a smaller step first: Seeing the captions on a demo video'.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (order the caption glasses with free returns), asking whether to offer it as a pilot at the end is the obvious next move before people see the study.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and the hint says exactly what respondents will see and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect emails from people ready to order is entirely my call as the founder.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: My step was 'order the caption glasses with free returns' but the line respondents get is a generic 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.', which doesn't show them the step I typed, so it drifts a little from my offer.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Saving my answers and fixing the interviewer just before the study goes out is the right last step of the flow.
screens.why2: 'Lock and record the face Keel preselects' needs a second read, because 'face' (the AI interviewer's look) is Keel's word and not mine, and the heading 'Save your answers' says nothing about a face.
screens.why3: It is about my own study and what my respondents will see, which I can decide.
screens.why4: The pick bundles two acts, locking and recording, and accepting Keel's preselected face, so I cannot save without also taking the default face.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed about AirCaps, the wearer or the price.
screens.instead: Save your answers -- and who should ask the questions? (Keep the interviewer Keel picked / Choose a different interviewer)

screens.why1: Choosing how the study link reaches people is the natural last step after saving my answers, just before I send it out.
screens.why2: The options read plainly, but the heading 'New link' doesn't say it's asking how respondents will take the interview, so I'd need a second look to see what I'm choosing.
screens.why3: I know my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can easily judge which format they can actually use.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete, but 'A face on video asks each question aloud' doesn't say it's captioned, which makes it look unusable for my deaf respondents.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or study is changed or leaked; this screen is only about delivery format.
screens.instead: How should people take this interview? Read and tap (they read each question and tap or type) / AI interviewer (a face on video asks each question aloud, with captions on screen; they answer by talking, typing or tapping) / Let them choose

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits under the title with its deciding number beside it (1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month), though as founder I'd have expected Price at 0 of 7 to be the headline.
screens.why_b2: Each card's count, its 7 people and its bar of 5 of 7 are plain, but the numbering skips from 4 to 6 and the verdict's 'per person a month' differs from the card's wording, so I read it twice.
screens.why_b3: Price and Buyer and payer read as mine, but my cost estimate was $200 to $1,500 a year and here it is about 12 lost conversations a month, which I recognise but did not type that way.
screens.why_b4: The status lines ('they value it below your price', 'they lose less today than you estimated') describe the result but never say what to do next, such as testing a lower price or a different segment.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card, but a 7-person read is stated flatly as 'they lose less today than you estimated' with no note that the sample is small.
screens.instead: Not holding up on price: none of 7 would pay $599 up front or $20 a month, and only 1 of 7 loses a dozen conversations a month. With 7 people this is a warning, not a verdict, so test a lower entry price or the heaviest-use wearers before changing the idea.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up, smaller than you think' sits directly over '1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells with 1 for and 6 against is easy to read, but the unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled share-frame wording, and the bar marker at 5 on a 0-15 conversations axis makes me look twice to work out whether 5 is people or conversations.
screens.why_b3: I recognise my count of about 12 conversations a month, but the belief tacks on a redundant ': conversations they lost the thread of' and loses the plain sense of what I meant.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates that they are below my low and points me to the Price card, but it doesn't say what this means for AirCaps, for example that most people put their loss at 4 to 8 conversations, so my pitch shouldn't lean on a big existing loss.
screens.why_b5: The count line shows n=7 and calls it 'a lean, not a call', but the headline 'they lose less today than you estimated' reads as a flat claim about deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in general.
screens.instead: Not holding up among these 7: most lost the thread of 4 to 8 conversations last month, against your 12, and only 1 reached it; a small group, so treat it as a lean and build the case on what following more is worth, not on a large loss today.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside the deciding numbers, 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each step, so I know it failed and why in one line.
screens.why_b2: Each ladder shows its counts band by band with for or against marked, my $599 and $20 sit on the low edge of a band, and the bar of 5 of 7 is drawn under each, so what is counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Price and the belief reads $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan, which is the glasses price and Pro plan I charge, named as AirCaps.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me 6 of 7 cluster at $250 to under $599, which hints at where the price lands, but it doesn't say what to do about the up-front price or the monthly plan, and it sends the try-before-you-buy theme to another tab when the quotes here (borrow a pair for a matinee, demo it on a noisy walk) already show it.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" says the count is low, and calling the result "not holding up" at 0 of 7 claims nothing the answers can't carry; the only blur is that the So line drops "optional" from the plan.
screens.instead: Say: none of 7 would pay $599 up front, and 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599; the $20 plan is optional, so judge it apart; several want to try a pair in their own hard moment first, so test a lower up-front price or a borrow-first offer.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not reached' sits right beside its deciding number, 0 of 7 named your price or more, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The bars all read 0 and the strip shows 5 ghost cells against 7 people, so I need a second look to see that the floor of 5 is the bar and that nobody was asked at all.
screens.why_b3: I never typed this belief; Keel derived it from my $599 and $20 a month, so the price is mine but the 'money they already spend on this' line is Keel's wording.
screens.why_b4: The So line says only that the card waits until 5 reach my price, which is mechanically true but does not say that price is the blocker to fix first.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7 people, shows n plainly, and says the card decides nothing.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of 7 would pay $599, so nobody was asked where the money would come from; settle Price first, since six of them put it at $250 to $599.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 decided alone against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The four answers with their counts, the 7 people, and the marker at 5 on the strip are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, with the wearer deciding and nobody else having to agree, is the line I picked, and the bar line repeats it in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the tally; it doesn't say what this means for the idea, for example that I can sell straight to the wearer and that the commercial problem lies in price and spend, not in who signs off.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 7 a lean, but the So line states "They decide alone on purchases like this" as fact, and "something like this" may mean a free phone app rather than $599 glasses, so the result can't carry that flat a claim.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean: 6 of 7 paid alone the last time (Walter needed his wife), so pitch the wearer directly rather than their family; but the last purchase was probably a cheap app, so check this again at $599.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes and the bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each answer over the 7 who answered, and the strip puts my bar at 5 with 6 for and 1 against, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Commitment and says my belief in my own words: order the caption glasses with free returns.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' points at a next step but leaves 'it' unclear (an order? a fitting?), and with no price in the question I can't tell whether these six would actually pay $599.
screens.why_b5: The card names n and calls it 'a lean, not a call', but 'Book them into it' treats six hypothetical yeses to a step with no price stated as ready orders, and the rule line's 'after try the caption glasses' slips its grammar.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 said they'd order with free returns, though the question named no price. Book these six for a fitting and quote $599 there to see who still says yes.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the deciding numbers: 0 of 7 at $599 up front and 0 of 7 at $20 a month, against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The line is Price, and the belief is my ladder as I'd say it: $599 for the glasses, then the optional $20/month Pro plan.
screens.why_b4: The screen is headed 'When a line fails' but never says what this means for AirCaps; I have to infer the moves from the group names myself, such as pushing a try-first offer or proving crosstalk.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible throughout: 7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka named as never seeing it, and each quote carries its own price bands, so nothing claims beyond the seven who answered.
screens.why_b6: I learned things I didn't type: people want to physically try a pair before paying even though I already offer 15-day free returns, so that offer isn't landing. They also judge worth on multi-speaker crosstalk such as audience questions and eleven people at lunch, and the one-sided-loss and lip-read-and-laugh-late folks anchor at $0.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 0 of 7 would pay $599; the two that move it are a hands-on trial (your 15-day free return isn't reaching them, so say it louder or offer demo pairs) and proof it keeps up with many people talking at once; try those before cutting the price.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is plain why they'd check I actually talk with hearing people before asking me about it.
screens.why2: Short and in my own words; "hearing people" is how we deaf and hard-of-hearing folks say it.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people in a week -- at work, the shop, the doctor.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and no escape is right here.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment (talking with hearing people every week) and leaks nothing of the product.
screens.why6: The question says well, but the spoken form leaves off "Yes or no." that the screener template calls for, so the choice is never read out.
screens.instead: Do you talk with hearing people face to face every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after the weekly-conversation gate, showing me the idea before the questions about it makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Live captions and eye contact are everyday words for me, and the card reads cleanly the first time, though 'would have you read' is a little stiff.
screens.why3: Reading captions while trying to keep eye contact with a hearing person is exactly what I deal with every week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The idea is shown on purpose as an Imagine card, in plain terms, with no inside product or role language leaking through.
screens.why6: Three short sentences with no symbols or parentheses, easy to take in when heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions of people nearby. When someone near you talks, you see their words inside the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words and still keep eye contact.

screens.why1: After asking if I talk with hearing people every week, asking how often I lose the conversation is the obvious next thing, and it's my everyday problem.
screens.why2: I understand it, but 'stop following the thread of' is a clumsy way to end a question and I'd read it twice; I'd say 'got lost in' or 'couldn't keep up with'.
screens.why3: It happens to me all the time, but I don't count it, so a number for a whole month would be a guess, more so for the quick chats at the shop or work.
screens.why4: A box for the number, None for a month when it never happened, and I can't recall for when I truly don't know are clear and separate.
screens.why5: No product, company or odd labels for people come through; it's just about conversations I lose track of.
screens.why6: It's short and has one escape, but 'stop following the thread of' heard once is a mouthful with a dangling 'of', and I'd want it on the captions.
screens.why7: It's one count of conversations, for one person, over one month, with no percent and no 'lose' or 'miss'; any number can fall above or below the founder's low, and the one required escape is there.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations did you get lost in or stop being able to follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking what the glasses are worth makes sense right after the idea card, but it comes straight after one question about lost conversations and sits under a 'What you do today' kicker, so it feels abrupt and mislabelled.
screens.why2: 'What would AirCaps be worth to you up front' and then 'a month' are plain words I'd use about hearing aids and their plans.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids, batteries and captioning apps, so I can say from my own wallet what glasses like these would be worth to me.
screens.why4: The bands are complete and don't overlap, but '$250 to under $599' stands out: $599 looks like a shop sticker price, not a round amount I'd think in, so it hints at what they plan to charge.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own name and description reach me, and 'up front' and 'a month' are how I'd talk about paying for a device and its plan.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it's one short question, four options at a time, then two, with the single 'I can't say'; the two-step monthly plan follows the same pattern, so it's easy to hold.
screens.why7: Both ladders are one up-front step then one monthly plan step, each with six rungs in the price alone, an edge at what reads as the founder's low ($599, $20), bands on both sides, 'I wouldn't pay for this' as an answer, and 'I can't say' as the one escape.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $600 · $600 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this (keeping the edge at the founder's low only if $599 really is their low)

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking what would push it higher is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: It plays back my own range in plain money words, and asks a simple question I'd get on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make captions worth more to me, like keeping up in a loud restaurant or a group at work, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps is the name from the idea card I was shown, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and '$250 to $600' says cleanly aloud.

screens.why1: Right after I've put a price on AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd have had to talk anyone into it, like my husband or my insurance, though the counter jumping from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5 is a little odd.
screens.why2: Short and in everyday words, and since I've just seen the AirCaps card I'd take 'something like this' to mean hearing aids or a captioning gadget I've bought.
screens.why3: I remember paying for my hearing aids and the caption phone, so I can say from my own life whether anyone else had a say.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from 'on my own' to 'someone else's call', they don't overlap, they're in my words, and 'I can't say' covers me if I'd rather not get into it.
screens.why5: Nothing of the company's plan or its own terms for people reaches me; it just asks who had to agree.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold, then the escape, though 'someone else had to agree' and 'someone else's call' sound close on the captions and the spoken switch from 'I decided' to 'You decided' is slightly off the screen's words.
screens.why7: With nobody else tested the item asks about anyone else, gives the fixed four in order from alone to someone else's call, has 'Someone else' as the second row, and keeps 'I can't say' apart, so one answer can support it and three can refute it.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for something like hearing aids or a captioning device, did anyone else have to agree? I decided on my own · Someone else had to agree · Several people had to agree · It was someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: After asking what it's worth to me and who else would have to agree, it makes sense to finish by asking whether I'd actually order them, though the kicker calling it 'What you do today' is a little off for a what-if.
screens.why2: 'Caption glasses' and 'free returns' are words I'd use myself, and I'd get it on the first read or hearing.
screens.why3: Whether I'd order a pair of glasses that caption the people talking to me is my own decision, and one I could answer right away.
screens.why4: There's a firm yes, a soft yes that says what I'd want first (to try them on in person, which is different from ordering and sending them back), probably not, and no, so whatever I'd really say is there.
screens.why5: It's the founder's step, ordering with free returns, and it only uses the glasses the idea card just showed me, so nothing slips in that I wasn't meant to see.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four options I can hold in my head when I hear them, though hearing 'the caption glasses' twice is a little wordy.
screens.why7: The first option is a yes to the founder's own paid step, and the second is a yes to a free smaller step (trying them in person) that isn't just the step again. Two options count for and two against, with No as the floor and no escape option, as the card requires.
